newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Foreign investment in Taiwan up 17 pct in Jan-Apr.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in Taiwan up 17 pct in Jan-Apr.

text.p: Foreign investment in Taiwan rose a year-on-year 17 percent in January-April, reflecting efforts to transform the island into an Asia-Pacific operations hub for transnational firms, officials said on Thursday.
In the first four months of 1997, foreign investment totalled US$594 million, up 17 percent from $507 million in the 1996 period, the Investment Commission announced.

Foreign investment in the electronics and electrical appliance industries, which topped the investment sector with 35 percent of the pie, accounted for $208 million, up 45 percent year-on-year, it said.

Investment in the next biggest sector, the finance and insurance industry, fell 45 percent. Investment in international trade grew 96 percent, that in services 313 percent, and chemicals manufacturing a dramatic 664 percent.
Broken down in terms of origin, investment from Japan rose 55 percent to $196.4 million, followed by unspecified "other regions", which fell 14 percent to $189.9 million.
Investment from the United States grew 51 percent to $82.4 million. That from Europe surged 188 percent to $66.3 million and investment from Hong Kong fell 20 percent to $15.9 million.
Taiwan's own overseas investments -- excluding that in the rival Chinese communist mainland -- fell 11 percent to $707 million in January-April from $795 million in the 1996 period.
January-April investment by Taiwan in unspecified "other regions" -- mainly Central American tax havens -- dropped 30 percent to $438 million.
Taiwan's U.S. investments rose 31 percent to $98.8 million.
Investment in Southeast Asia surged in January-April as Taiwan firms have been urged by the government to diversify their investments away from the Chinese mainland.

Worried that Taiwan firms could become too dependent on the island's principal adversary, leaving Taiwan politically vulnerable, Taipei launched a "southbound policy" in 1993 to promote investments in Southeast Asia instead of China.
Since mid-1996, Taipei has intensified its efforts to limit investment in China, vowing to punish firms that route capital secretly through third countries into unauthorised projects.
January-April investment in Singapore rocketed an annual 707 percent to $48.3 million, followed by Vietnam, which surged 84 percent to $41 million.
Investment in the Philippines leapt 148 percent to $26.4 million and that in Indonesia shot up 3,700 percent to $25.8 million. But investment in Malaysia and Thailand fell 48 percent and 22 percent.
Overseas investments focused on international trade, finance and insurance, transport, electronics and electrical appliance and metal manufacturing industries, it said.
